svg.title: 24 Game in L^

text.tspan: Write a program that randomly chooses and displays four digits, each from
The program should prompt for the player to enter an arithmetic expression
using just those, and all of those four digits, used exactly once each. The
program should check then evaluate the expression.
The goal is for the player to enter an expression that (numerically)
- Only the following operators/functions are allowed: multiplication,
- Division should use floating point or rational arithmetic, etc, to
- Brackets are allowed, if using an infix expression evaluator.
- Forming multiple digit numbers from the supplied digits is disallowed.
(So an answer of 12+12 when given 1, 2, 2, and 1 is wrong).
- The order of the digits when given does not have to be preserved.
Reader reads the written expression and counts as it goes. Both the position
and "how many times each digit was used" are fields of the instance, so there
The mutual recursion (expr -> term -> factor -> expr) goes through self^.
this^^ names the enclosing literal, not a sibling member, so it does not
reach one. A def^'s members see each other (14.7改), so a ring of them needs
Meeting a spelling it cannot read, it lowers ok and answers 0. No error value
is made, because this is the input's mistake and not the writer's -- the same
line 14.19 draws when it answers an empty string outside the range it holds
# The multiset of digits used. 1..9 index it directly
# The character here, spaces skipped. "" once the text is spent
# One digit, or an expression in brackets.
# A written 12 does not become 12 because this takes one character only
# the if^d < 1 or^ d > 9 { above holds d to 1..9, so
# there is no nil check to make: this need not be self^.used[d] ?+= 1
# The whole expression. Anything left unread is the player's mistake
# Whether the four dealt and the four used are the same multiset. Each takes a
# table of counts, one per digit of 1..9
# narrowing the range is what removes the nil check
# L^ cannot tell from rng.range(1, 9) that d is within 1..9,
# so the if^1 <= d <= 9 {} around it is what says so.
# Without the narrowing it has to be written this way:
# which is shorter, and says a nil^ may be reached where none ever
# is -- and would swallow one that arrived from somewhere unnoticed.
"Enter an expression using each of them once, or an empty line to stop."
"That is not an expression I can read."
"Use each of the four digits exactly once."
# / is real division, so 8/(3-8/3) does not land on exactly 24.
# But = takes the error of a real into account, so comparing
# directly is fine. To pick the width yourself there is the member
# eq (not needed here), or round it with value.round().
